extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, social criticism, and literary/cultural theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic account of how democratic vs aristocratic social conditions shape the production, form, and language of the arts and literature; includes practical consequences for craftsmen, artists, authors, and public monuments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic craftsmanship values
rubrics_metrics.description: In ages of privilege the practice of almost all the arts becomes a privilege; artisans form a distinct class concerned with reputation as well as fortune, and the object of the arts is to manufacture as well as possible—not with the greatest despatch, or at the lowest rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guild-like social ties make each artisan aim for the best possible workmanship; quality, durability, and perfection are prioritized over speed or low price. Example: when only the wealthy had watches, they were almost all very good ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic craftsmanship incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: When professions are open to all and practitioners are numerous and transient, each workman strives to gain the greatest quantity of money at least cost; the will of the customer becomes the primary limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are two ways to lower prices: (1) invent shorter / more ingenious production methods, or (2) mass-produce similar but lower-value goods. Democratic incentives direct intellectual faculties toward speed, economy, or diminished intrinsic quality; consumers likewise accept imperfect goods rather than go without (example: crude, widely available watches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass-production reduces intrinsic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Among democratic populations artisans either invent faster/better methods or diminish the intrinsic qualities of goods to sell them cheaply in large quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tendency produces a large quantity of imperfect commodities and trains consumers to content themselves with these commodities; excellent workmanship becomes rarer and exceptional craftsmen have fewer opportunities to display their full abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation and imposture in the marketplace
rubrics_metrics.description: Handicraftsmen in democracies often give commodities attractive qualities which they do not in reality possess, using devices of imposture to satisfy social vanity and imitative desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such impostures can be so successful they defeat their purpose (example: imitation diamonds); architectural façades may mimic marble with painted wood (example: buildings at the Narrows near New York). This reflects a broader democratic appetite for appearance over substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine arts shift: appearance and the real over the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic conditions tend to withdraw imitative arts from the delineation of the soul toward that of the body, substituting the representation of motion and sensation for sentiment and thought, and favoring the real over the ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Painters increasingly copy trivial details of private life and realistic anatomy instead of aspiring to idealized representations (contrast: Raphael's idealizing aspiration vs David's fidelity to nature). Result: more numerous but lower-merit artworks (many pretty or elegant works rather than a few grand ones; statues in plaster rather than bronze).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public monumentalism under democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Although individuals are relatively powerless in democracies, the State is powerful and apt to erect gigantic public monuments; democracies therefore produce both many insignificant works and occasional very large-scale public undertakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large state-sponsored projects (e.g., planned capitals, capitol buildings) reflect collective imagination and centralized power but do not necessarily indicate real societal greatness, civilization, or prosperity (examples: Capitol planning, Mexican temples, Roman aqueducts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocratic literary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocratic societies a small literate class establishes precise and traditional canons for literature; style and form are as important as thought, with polished, measured, and uniform diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the same small class writes and reads, they can concert rules and perpetuate them; literary production emphasizes perfection and detail, often producing works aimed at connoisseurs. Danger: an isolated literary aristocracy may develop an aristocratic jargon remote from common speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic literary characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature in democratic ages lacks permanent conventional rules; style is often fantastic, incorrect, overburdened, loose, vehement and bold; authors prefer rapid execution, short works, wit over erudition, and imagination over profundity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers in democracies are numerous, heterogeneous, often with limited time and education; they demand books that are easily procured, quickly read, and striking. Writers therefore aim to astonish and stir passions rather than to perfect detail or cultivate learned subtlety; exceptions of great writers exist but are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization of literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy introduces a trading spirit into literature: authors may secure a meagre reputation and large fortune cheaply by pleasing a wide market; literature is often treated as a trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mass of readers and their continual craving for novelty guarantee sales for books that are liked, not necessarily esteemed; democratic literature is thereby 'infested' with many who view letters as a commercial activity (the journalist is noted as the most genuinely 'American' author of the moment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical study as corrective in democratic societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Study of Greek and Latin literature is especially useful in democratic nations to counterbalance the defects of democratic literature—care for detail, pursuit of ideal beauty, and learned discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient literature exemplifies painstaking craftsmanship and ideal conception useful to refresh and correct democratic writers; however, classics should not be imposed universally—rather they should be available in excellent institutions for those destined to cultivate letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic influence on language
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic social conditions accelerate linguistic change: new words proliferate (often from party jargon, mechanical arts, or trade), old words shift in sense, and phraseology may diverge from the mother-country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority-driven language change tends to favor terms useful for business, party politics, and public administration, while vocabulary for metaphysics and theology may decline. Examples: differences between American educated speech and British, and the tendency in democracies to adopt practical, trade-related neologisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional confluence produces brilliant but ephemeral literary epochs
rubrics_metrics.description: During gradual transitions from aristocracy to democracy there are moments when literary geniuses of both regimes converge, producing transient, brilliant epochs that combine order and variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such hybrid periods can be fertile and animated without confusion (example: French literature of the eighteenth century), but they are historically transient and do not define the long-term character of either regime.
